passages.where: The psalm begins with the confession of faith, that God is good to the pure in heart, and then admits how nearly the singer lost it. He had kept his heart clean and suffered for it, while the arrogant were healthy, well fed and at ease. The site's note points out that the man saying this probably stood in the temple choir: it is a worship leader who nearly slipped.

Thinking harder only made it heavier. The turn comes when he goes into God's sanctuary and sees where the path of the wicked ends. He does not find his answer by pretending the unfairness was not there; he brings his question into God's house.

Jeremiah says God is righteous and in the same breath takes him to court: why does the way of the wicked prosper? God does not answer with an explanation. The note on the chapter says he answers with a harder assignment: if running with men has worn you out, how will you race with horses?

The prophet's book opens with a complaint, not a sermon. He has cried out about violence and injustice, the law is paralyzed, and God seems not to listen. Scripture keeps this protest in God's own book, word for word.

Habakkuk takes his stand on the watchtower to wait for an answer. God tells him to write the vision plainly, because it waits for its appointed time and will surely come, and then sets the proud man beside the righteous who will live by faith. The answer is not that justice is quick, but that it is certain.

The Teacher has watched the wicked honored at their own funerals and seen that justice delayed encourages evil. He names it plainly: righteous people get what the wicked deserve, and the wicked get what the righteous deserve. He does not explain it, and he commends enjoying the days God gives rather than pretending the world is fair.

An old man counsels the faithful not to fret or envy when the wicked prosper. He repeats the same lesson in many forms across forty verses: trust, commit, be still, wait. Fretting, he says in the next verse, only leads to harm; the stillness he asks for is trust in God, not the pretense that nothing is wrong.

Workers who bore the heat of the whole day see latecomers paid the same and grumble. The site's note says no one was cheated: the first workers got the fair wage they agreed to, and their complaint is that others were treated generously. The parable ends on a question left for the hearer, and it turns the cry of unfairness back on the one who makes it.

Jesus tells of a widow who keeps coming to a judge who fears no one. The note is clear that the parable works by contrast: God is nothing like that judge, and he hears his chosen ones who cry to him day and night. Then Jesus turns the question around and asks whether he will find faith when he comes.

Under the altar John sees those who were killed for the word of God, and they cry out to the Lord, holy and true, asking how long until he judges. Their cry is not rebuked. Each is given a white robe and told to rest a little longer.

Paul tells believers not to repay evil for evil and not to avenge themselves, but to leave room for God's wrath. The note on the chapter adds that this never means staying where someone is hurting you or keeping silent about harm. Justice is not cancelled; it is handed to the one who can do it rightly.

misread.taken: People who are suffering something unjust are often told, sometimes within days of it, that God meant it for good, as if the wrong done to them were not really wrong, or as if they ought already to see the purpose in it.
misread.says: Joseph names what his brothers did as evil. He says these words many years later, as the one who was wronged, looking back when he could see what came of it; no one said them to him in the pit or in prison. The site's note on the chapter calls the verse much loved and often misused: it does not call evil good, it is never a line to hand to someone in fresh grief, and it is never a reason to explain away abuse.

misread.taken: The saying that a man reaps what he sows is often used as a law of payback: if your life has gone badly, you must have sown it, and if someone has wronged you, life will soon pay them back.
misread.says: Paul is speaking of a whole life sown to the flesh or to the Spirit, and the harvest he names is eternal life. The site's note on the chapter says the verse does not mean that every hardship is the harvest of a person's own sin: Job's friends said that, and God said they were wrong. Nor does it promise that the wicked will be paid back on our schedule. It is a call to keep doing good without growing weary.

whole: Unfairness has a particular sting. The colleague who cut corners is promoted. The family member who did the least for a dying parent inherits the most. The person who hurt you seems to sleep well while you lie awake. Sometimes the unfairness is larger and has no face: a child born sick, a town where the jobs left, a life that was ordinary until one bad day. Underneath the hurt comes a quieter question that many Christians are ashamed to ask out loud, which is whether faithfulness was worth it at all, and whether God is keeping the books he said he would keep.

Scripture does not hush that question. It gives it to us in the words of a temple singer whose feet nearly slipped, a prophet who took God to court, another who stood on a watchtower demanding an answer, a Teacher who said the righteous get what the wicked deserve, and the martyrs under the altar crying out how long. Much of the Bible's wisdom teaches that the righteous flourish and the wicked fall, and the Bible itself admits that life often looks the other way. Job's friends tried to close the gap by deciding that sufferers must deserve it, and God said they had not spoken rightly. The cause of the ache is real: the world is not yet as God means it to be, and justice is often delayed.

That shapes what wisdom looks like. It refuses two false comforts at once: that the wrong is secretly good, and that the books will balance in this life if we wait. It takes the protest to God rather than swallowing it, because the psalms and the prophets show that the complaint is itself a kind of prayer. It refuses revenge, not because the wrong does not matter, but because God has said he will repay and we cannot do it rightly. It also watches its own heart, because the grumbling workers in the vineyard show how easily a sense of unfairness turns into resentment of God's generosity to someone else. And it keeps doing good, which Paul says is the harder and better harvest.

The Christian hope here is not that the world is fair. It is that God is just, that the vision will surely come, and that the one who suffered most unjustly of all, Christ himself, did not answer evil with evil but entrusted himself to the God who judges rightly. The singer of Psalm 73 found his answer in the sanctuary, and what he found was not an explanation but a presence: God holding his right hand. Many questions stay open until the end. What the faithful are given in the meantime is not the scorecard but the God who keeps it.
sit: Where are you keeping a quiet score against someone, or against God, and what would it look like to bring that score into his presence instead of carrying it alone?

prayer.lead: The end of Psalm 73, prayed by a man who had nearly given up because the wicked seemed to win. Pray it on the day the unfairness is loudest.
